opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be here.

What I really valued about IIT Madras was how strong the foundations were. The curriculum put a lot of weight on the fundamentals: algorithms, data structures, discrete math, theory of computation, operating systems, compilers. At the time, as an undergrad, you sometimes wonder why you're spending so much time proving things about automata or working through complexity, but in hindsight that rigor has been incredibly useful. When you move into research, especially in a fast-moving area like machine learning, the specific tools and frameworks change every few years, but the core way of thinking about problems stays with you.

The other thing was the peer group. You're surrounded by really motivated, sharp people, and a lot of the learning happened outside the classroom, late-night discussions, working on assignments together, programming contests, side projects. That environment pushes you to raise your own bar.

And I'd say there was a healthy balance between theory and systems. You got to build real things, write a compiler, work on networking or databases, while also understanding why things work the way they do. That combination of being comfortable with math and comfortable writing code turned out to be exactly what you need in AI research. A lot of what we did later, including the work on language models, really sits at that intersection: having a good mathematical intuition for what a model is doing, and then actually being able to engineer it at scale.

So for me it was less about any one course and more about the foundation it gave me, and the confidence to pick up new areas on my own, which is what eventually led me toward natural language processing and machine learning in grad school.

r001.rationale: The candidate says IIT Madras provided strong foundations and lists coursework spanning algorithms, theory, systems, and math, clearly crediting the curriculum’s breadth with building a broad foundation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what I valued most about IIT Madras was that the curriculum was really fundamentals-first. We spent a lot of time on things like algorithms, theory of computation, discrete math, operating systems, compilers, and at the time I sometimes wondered why I needed to prove the correctness of some algorithm or understand how a page table works when what I really wanted to do was build things. But in hindsight that grounding was incredibly useful. When I later moved into machine learning and NLP, a lot of the work was about understanding systems at a deep level, reasoning about complexity, about what's actually computable or learnable, and those fundamentals transferred directly.

The second thing was that it was quite rigorous but also gave you a lot of freedom. The core courses were demanding, but there was room to take electives, do projects, and go explore on your own. I remember some of my most formative experiences were not in lectures but in late-night project work with classmates, trying to get something to run, debugging, arguing about design choices. The peer group was honestly a big part of the education. You're surrounded by people who are very sharp and very motivated, and you learn as much from them as from the faculty.

And then the third thing, which I appreciate more now as a professor, is that the faculty there cared about getting students to think rather than memorize. There were a few professors who would ask these open-ended questions in class that didn't have a clean answer, and that was my first exposure to what research actually feels like, sitting with uncertainty and trying to make progress anyway. That planted the seed for wanting to do a PhD, which I don't think I'd have considered otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response describes a curriculum spanning algorithms, theory, discrete math, operating systems, and compilers, and says that grounding transferred directly to later work in machine learning and NLP.
